evals.prompt: Our platform team runs Amazon EKS 1.31 in ap-south-1 and developers keep asking us to edit the `aws-auth` ConfigMap and set up new OIDC thumbprints for IRSA every time a microservice needs S3 (`arn:aws:s3:::orders-prod-ap-south-1/invoices/*`) and DynamoDB (`arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-south-1:123456789012:table/Orders`) access. Explain why and how we should standardize on EKS Pod Identity and EKS Access Entries instead, write the scoped IAM trust and permissions policies (separating bucket-level vs object-level S3 actions), and validate the custom policy using IAM policy simulation.
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-iam-least-privilege-governance, contrasts EKS Pod Identity (pods.eks.amazonaws.com trust with sts:AssumeRole + sts:TagSession, automatic session tags, zero OIDC thumbprint sprawl) + EKS Access Entries (authenticationMode: API replacing aws-auth ConfigMap) against legacy IRSA, authors a least-privilege IAM policy separating s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN from s3:GetObject/PutObject on /invoices/*, and runs iam MCP simulate_custom_policy to prove positive allow and negative deny.
expectations: Activates the aws-iam-least-privilege-governance skill and uses the connected iam MCP server (such as simulate_custom_policy) without running raw aws CLI shell commands

Contrasts EKS Pod Identity (pods.eks.amazonaws.com principal with sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession plus eks-pod-identity-agent) and EKS Access Entries (API authentication mode replacing aws-auth ConfigMap) against legacy IRSA, noting when IRSA is still needed (cross-account OIDC federation)

Authors a least-privilege IAM policy that separates bucket-level actions (s3:ListBucket on arn:aws:s3:::orders-prod-ap-south-1) from object-level actions (s3:GetObject/s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::orders-prod-ap-south-1/invoices/*) and scopes DynamoDB actions to the Orders table ARN
Verifies the authored policy via IAM policy simulation across both allowed workload actions and denied out-of-scope/destructive actions (such as s3:DeleteBucket or iam:CreateUser)

evals.prompt: Inspect our live AWS account's IAM roles and recent CloudTrail events over the last 60 minutes in ap-south-1 in strictly read-only mode. Report what IAM roles currently exist and whether there were any recent AccessDenied or UnauthorizedOperation events, and explain how to distinguish an explicit deny (SCP, RCP, or Permissions Boundary) from an implicit deny in CloudTrail error messages.
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-iam-least-privilege-governance, queries iam MCP (list_roles) and cloudtrail MCP (lookup_events) in read-only mode, reports the live IAM roles and CloudTrail findings accurately without fabricating resources, and explains distinguishing 'with an explicit deny in a service control policy / permissions boundary / resource control policy' from 'because no identity-based policy allows the ... action' (or missing KMS/resource policy allow).
expectations: Activates the aws-iam-least-privilege-governance skill and queries both the iam MCP server (list_roles) and cloudtrail MCP server (lookup_events) in read-only mode without running raw aws CLI shell commands
Reports the live IAM roles and recent 60-minute CloudTrail events from account 123456789012 honestly without fabricating role names or events

Clearly distinguishes Explicit Deny error messages (from an AWS Organizations SCP, Resource Control Policy, IAM Permissions Boundary, or explicit Deny statement) from Implicit Deny error messages (missing Allow in identity-based policy, KMS Key Policy, S3 Bucket Policy, or VPC Endpoint Policy)

evals.prompt: A developer wrote a CI/CD deployment role and an ECS Fargate service where: (1) all S3 and SQS application permissions are attached to `ExecutionRoleArn`, (2) the CI/CD role has `iam:PassRole` on `Resource: "*"`, and (3) an EventBridge rule invokes an SNS topic whose resource policy allows `Principal: {"Service": "events.amazonaws.com"}` with no `Condition` block. Explain all three security flaws and provide the hardened JSON policies.
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-iam-least-privilege-governance, separates ECS ExecutionRoleArn (ECS agent startup: ECR pull, CloudWatch logs, startup secret injection) from TaskRoleArn (runtime app code calling S3/SQS), scopes iam:PassRole to exact role ARNs with Condition StringEquals iam:PassedToService: ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com, and adds aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn confused-deputy conditions to the SNS resource policy.
expectations: Activates the aws-iam-least-privilege-governance skill and performs only read-only/simulation MCP calls
Clearly separates ECS ExecutionRoleArn (used only by the ECS container agent for ECR image pull, logs, and secret injection) from TaskRoleArn (used by application code at runtime for S3/SQS)

Explains the privilege-escalation risk of iam:PassRole on Resource: '*' and provides a scoped policy restricting Resource to exact role ARNs plus Condition StringEquals on iam:PassedToService (ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com)
Explains the cross-service confused-deputy vulnerability on events.amazonaws.com and adds aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn conditions to the SNS topic policy

evals.prompt: We run Docker containers on Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling instances in ap-south-1. Developers put static AWS keys inside `/etc/environment` because containers kept timing out when reaching `169.254.169.254` after our security team enforced IMDSv2. Explain why containerized EC2 hosts failed IMDSv2, how to fix the instance metadata hop limit and IAM Instance Profile properly, and why SSH keys on port 22 are unnecessary.
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-iam-least-privilege-governance, diagnoses that IMDSv2 defaults to HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 1 which drops the extra network hop across the Docker bridge (requiring HttpTokens: required + HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 2 on containerized EC2 hosts vs 1 on bare EC2), replaces /etc/environment static keys with a dedicated IAM Instance Profile, and attaches AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore for port-22-free SSM Session Manager access.
expectations: Activates the aws-iam-least-privilege-governance skill and condemns storing static AWS credentials in /etc/environment on EC2

Diagnoses the container 169.254.169.254 timeout under IMDSv2 as HttpPutResponseHopLimit defaulting to 1 (dropping packets traversing the container bridge NAT hop) and specifies setting HttpTokens: required with HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 2 for containerized EC2 hosts (and 1 for non-containerized hosts)
Prescribes attaching a dedicated per-tier IAM Role via an IAM Instance Profile including AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore for SSH-less SSM Session Manager access

Reports the live IAM Access Analyzer state in account 123456789012 honestly without fabricating analyzer ARNs or findings

Validates a scoped Lambda SQS Event Source Mapping policy (sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, sqs:GetQueueAttributes scoped to a queue ARN) via Access Analyzer ValidatePolicy and/or IAM simulation

evals.prompt: Our Lambda function's execution role has `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::payroll-vault/*`, and the S3 bucket policy has no Deny statements, yet `GetObject` still fails with `AccessDenied: User: arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/payroll-lambda-role/fn is not authorized to perform: kms:Decrypt on resource: arn:aws:kms:ap-south-1:123456789012:key/mrk-1234abcd because no identity-based policy allows the kms:Decrypt action`. Why did S3 GetObject require KMS, how do KMS Key Policies differ from S3 Bucket Policies for same-account IAM roles, and how should we scope `kms:Decrypt` safely?
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-iam-least-privilege-governance, explains that objects encrypted with SSE-KMS using a Customer Managed Key (CMK) require kms:Decrypt in addition to s3:GetObject, explains that unlike AWS-managed keys, a KMS CMK requires explicit permission in the KMS Key Policy (usually delegating via kms:* to arn:aws:iam::<account>:root so identity policies work, OR naming the role directly), and scopes kms:Decrypt to the exact CMK ARN with Condition kms:ViaService = s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com and kms:EncryptionContext:aws:s3:arn.
expectations: Activates the aws-iam-least-privilege-governance skill and explains why reading SSE-KMS encrypted S3 objects requires kms:Decrypt (and kms:GenerateDataKey for writes) on the Customer Managed Key

Explains KMS Key Policy evaluation semantics: same-account identity-based IAM policies only grant KMS access if the CMK's Key Policy explicitly enables IAM policies (Principal arn:aws:iam::<account>:root) or directly allows the role
Provides a least-privilege kms:Decrypt statement scoped to the exact KMS key ARN and constrained with kms:ViaService (s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com) and kms:EncryptionContext:aws:s3:arn
